title: The Patriarch
dialogue: The afternoon sun casts long, harsh shadows across the carpet. The door opens. Vyktor does not walk in. He stands in the frame. His face is entirely blank.
monologue: When Vyktor is angry, he clips his words. When he is afraid, he stops speaking entirely. He is not speaking.

narrative.text: Stefan Morvec is here. He bypassed the security checkpoint at the gate. The guards simply... let his car through. He is waiting in the anteroom.
Stefan Morvec has not left the Aldenmoor estate in eleven years. He did not attend the inauguration. He did not attend the state funerals. If he is in Ashenmere, the earth has shifted.

morvec_arrival.monologue: He sent his son to threaten me in Week 16. Aleksei was a dog barking at the fence. Stefan is the man who owns the fence. He has come to close the gate.

choices.text: Send him in. And Vyktor? Stay outside. I will handle this alone.

reactions.text: Vyktor hesitates for a fraction of a second. Then he nods and steps back.

choices.text: Send him in. Stay by the door.

narrative.text: The heavy oak doors close with a soft click. Stefan Morvec enters. He leans heavily on a silver-tipped cane. His breathing is shallow, papery. He looks like a gust of wind could kill him.
Chancellor. Your office feels colder than I remember. Though it has been a long time since I walked these halls. Halvek kept the thermostat too high. He liked to sweat. A nervous man.

choices.text: You bypassed my security, Stefan. What do you want?

narrative.text: Stefan Morvec enters. He leans heavily on a silver-tipped cane. He pauses, looking at Vyktor standing rigidly by the door. Morvec smiles. It is a terrifying expression.

Chancellor. And Mr. Reznik — I remember your father. He worked in the census office in Dravenhollow. A very precise man. It is good that you are here. A Chancellor should not have to face old men alone.

choices.text: Get to the point, Stefan. Why are you in my office?

narrative.text: Morvec slowly walks to the large map of Veltria on the wall. He traces the border of Dravenhollow with a trembling, liver-spotted finger.

Do you know what happens to a house when the foundation shifts, Katerin? The roof does not fall immediately. The doors simply stop closing. The windows crack. The warmth escapes. And then, one winter, you freeze.
My son came to you months ago. Aleksei has a young man's temper. He believes power is something you take. He does not yet understand it is something you tend. Like a garden.
You have been pulling up the roots of my garden, Katerin. The banking regulations. The BNI purges. You are making the house very cold. I am here to ask you to close the windows.

the_foundation_speech.monologue: He doesn't yell. He doesn't have to. The 'garden' he is talking about is thirty percent of the Republic's GDP and half the military supply chain. He is calmly explaining that he will freeze the country to death if I don't stop.

choices.text: The house isn't shifting, Stefan. I am tearing it down. And I am building a new one.
If you try to freeze this country, I will have Dusek arrest you before your car reaches the gate.
What is the price to keep the heat on? Tell me exactly what you want.

narrative.text: Morvec stops tracing the map. He turns his head slowly. The polite grandfather vanishes. What is left is a predator that has survived three regimes.
Many people have tried to build new houses in Veltria. The ground here is very hard. It ruins their hands. And eventually, we bury them in it.
I enjoyed our dinner, Katerin. It is a shame we will not share another.
Morvec actually laughs. It is a dry, rasping sound that devolves into a cough. He leans heavily on his cane, catching his breath.
Dusek. The loyal Colonel. Do you know who paid for her brother's medical treatments in Orythia ten years ago? No. You don't read the ledgers deeply enough.
Behind you, Vyktor makes no sound. But in the glass reflection of the window, you see him. His jaw has gone rigid. His eyes are fixed on a point somewhere past the wall.
You cannot arrest the earth you stand on, Chancellor. By the time you sign the warrant, the ink will have run dry.

morvec_resolution_threaten.monologue: He is bluffing. He has to be bluffing about Dusek. But the coldness in my chest tells me I cannot afford to find out.

choices.text: We will see whose ink runs dry first. Leave.

narrative.text: The tension in his shoulders drops. The predator recedes, replaced once again by the reasonable, weary old man.
I want the Aldenmoor estate permanently exempted from the new taxation act. And I want my son, Aleksei, appointed to the oversight committee for the northern ports.
Do this, and the house stays warm. The factories stay open. The military gets their steel. We are a family, Katerin. Families take care of each other.

morvec_resolution_deal.monologue: I said it. No caveat. No threat about security checkpoints. There is nothing left to threaten him with and we both know it. The ports are his. I bought time with them. I will have to decide if time was worth the price.

choices.text: The arrangements will be made. Now get out of my office.

narrative.text: Morvec turns toward the door. Each step with the cane is a heavy, rhythmic thud against the hardwood floor. Thud. Drag. Thud. Drag. At the threshold, he stops. He does not turn. His voice, when it comes, is barely above a murmur.
My son wanted to come himself. I told him — let me speak with her first. Give her the chance to be reasonable. He is not a patient man, Katerin. And I will not always be here to hold his leash.
Good day, Chancellor. May God protect the Republic.
The doors close behind him. The silence he leaves in the room is heavier than when he entered.
